Exec scope "allowlist" silently maps to admin-only and the configured user allowlist is never enforced
body:
## Description

The exec capability config exposes a `scope` of `admin-only | allowlist | all` plus an `allowlist` array of Telegram user IDs:

```ts
// v1-src/config/schema.ts:312-319
scope: z
  .enum(["admin-only", "allowlist", "all"])
  .default("admin-only")
  .describe("Who can trigger exec tools"),
allowlist: z
  .array(z.number())
  .default([])
  .describe("Telegram user IDs allowed to use exec (when scope = allowlist)"),
```

But `resolveScope()` maps `allowlist` to the registry scope `admin-only`, and the `allowlist` array is never read anywhere in the exec module or its executors:

```ts
// v1-src/agent/tools/exec/module.ts:15-24
function resolveScope(scope: ExecConfig["scope"]): ToolScope {
  switch (scope) {
    case "admin-only":
      return "admin-only";
    case "allowlist":
      return "admin-only";
    case "all":
      return "always";
  }
}
```

The registry's `admin-only` branch authorizes against `config.telegram.admin_ids`, not `capabilities.exec.allowlist`. A grep of `v1-src/agent/tools/exec/` shows the only reference to `allowlist` is this `case` label; no executor (`run.ts`, `install.ts`, `service.ts`, `status.ts`) consults `execCfg.allowlist`. The configured allowlist is therefore dead configuration.

## Impact

The `allowlist` scope is a no-op that silently behaves identically to `admin-only`. An operator who sets `scope: "allowlist"` with a curated set of exec-authorized user IDs gets neither the intended behaviour nor any warning: the listed users are ignored, while access is granted to whoever is in `admin_ids` (a different, possibly broader set). Exec runs arbitrary shell commands on the host (see the `exec_run` tool and `bash -c` runner), so a mismatch between the operator's mental model and the enforced policy is a meaningful privilege/authorization hazard for a high-impact capability. Severity **high** because it governs arbitrary host command execution and fails silently.

## Required Fix

1. Actually enforce the allowlist: when `scope === "allowlist"`, authorize exec tool calls against `capabilities.exec.allowlist` (e.g. check `allowlist.includes(context.senderId)` in the executors or via a dedicated scope/permission), instead of collapsing to `admin-only`.
2. If the allowlist mode cannot be supported, fail loudly — reject the config at load time or log a prominent warning — rather than silently treating it as `admin-only`.
3. Add tests asserting that with `scope: "allowlist"`, a listed non-admin user is allowed and an unlisted (non-admin) user is denied.

## References

- CWE-863: Incorrect Authorization — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/863.html
- CWE-1188: Insecure Default Initialization of Resource — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1188.html
- OWASP Top 10 2021 A01: Broken Access Control — https://owasp.org/Top10/A01_2021-Broken_Access_Control/

ton_send tool has no bounce parameter and never passes it, so transfers default to bounceable
body:
## Description

The underlying `sendTon()` supports a `bounce` flag (defaulting to `false`) and forwards it to the message:

```ts
// v1-src/ton/transfer.ts:24
const { toAddress, amount, comment = "", bounce = false } = params;
// ...later passed to internal({ to, value, body, bounce })
```

but the `ton_send` tool neither exposes a `bounce` parameter nor passes one when calling `sendTon`:

```ts
// v1-src/agent/tools/ton/send.ts:19-33 (parameters — no `bounce`)
parameters: Type.Object({
  to: Type.String({ /* ... */ }),
  amount: Type.Number({ description: "Amount to send in TON (e.g., 1.5 for 1.5 TON)", minimum: 0.001 }),
  comment: Type.Optional(Type.String({ /* ... */ })),
}),
// v1-src/agent/tools/ton/send.ts:60
const txRef = await sendTon({ toAddress: to, amount, comment });
```

Because the tool always calls `sendTon` without `bounce`, every `ton_send` transfer uses the `bounce = false` default. (Note: the original finding referenced `transfer.ts:82` as ignoring the flag — that line does correctly forward `bounce`; the actual defect is in the `ton_send` tool wrapper, which provides no way to set it.) While `false` is the safer default for sending to uninitialized wallets, the flag is effectively unconfigurable: callers can never request a bounceable transfer (e.g. to a contract that should reject unexpected value), and the agent has no control over send semantics that real TON workflows depend on.

## Impact

The agent cannot choose bounce behaviour per transfer. The fixed non-bounceable default means value sent to a contract/address that *should* reject it (wrong state, not deployed as expected) will not be returned, and conversely there is no way to opt into bounceable sends where the protocol expects them. This is a correctness gap in the money-send path: the transfer's on-chain semantics are hard-coded and cannot match the recipient. Severity **medium** — it does not by itself leak funds in the common case, but it removes a safety control the lower layer already implements.

## Required Fix

1. Add an optional `bounce` boolean to the `ton_send` tool parameters (and likewise `jetton_send` where applicable) with a clearly documented default.
2. Forward it in the `sendTon({ toAddress, amount, comment, bounce })` call so the agent's choice is honoured.
3. Default to non-bounceable for plain wallet transfers but allow callers to enable bounce; add a test asserting the flag flows through to `sendTon`.

## References

- TON documentation: bounceable vs non-bounceable messages and addresses — https://docs.ton.org/develop/smart-contracts/guidelines/non-bounceable-messages
- CWE-665: Improper Initialization — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/665.html

WebUI accepts the auth token via ?token= query string (leaks via logs and browser history)
body:
## Description

The WebUI auth middleware accepts the bearer token from a `?token=` query-string parameter as a fallback for any `/api/*` request:

```ts
// v1-src/webui/server.ts:220-224
// 3. Check ?token= query param (fallback — backward compat)
const queryToken = c.req.query("token");
if (queryToken && safeCompare(queryToken, this.authToken)) {
  return next();
}
```

The same token also appears in the URL for the `/auth/exchange?token=...` flow (line 241) and is printed to logs as a URL hint that embeds the full token (`/auth/exchange?token=<token>`, near line 557). Query-string credentials are recorded in many places that headers and cookies are not: server/proxy/CDN access logs, browser history, `Referer` headers to third-party resources, and shoulder-surfable address bars.

## Impact

The long-lived WebUI auth token can leak through request logs, reverse-proxy logs, browser history, and `Referer` headers, allowing an attacker who reads any of those to authenticate to the WebUI (which controls the agent, memory, config, and wallet-adjacent setup routes). Severity **low** because the WebUI binds to `127.0.0.1` by default and the cookie/Bearer paths are preferred, but transmitting a credential in the URL is a well-known anti-pattern that should be removed or tightly scoped.

## Required Fix

1. Remove the `?token=` fallback for authenticated `/api/*` requests; require the `Authorization: Bearer` header or the HttpOnly session cookie instead.
2. Keep query-token use, if at all, strictly limited to the one-time `/auth/exchange` hand-off that immediately sets an HttpOnly cookie and redirects (stripping the token from the URL), and avoid logging the full token.
3. Add a test asserting that `/api/*` requests authenticated only via `?token=` are rejected.

## References

- CWE-598: Use of GET Request Method With Sensitive Query Strings — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/598.html
- CWE-522: Insufficiently Protected Credentials — https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/522.html
- OWASP: Information exposure through query strings in URL — https://owasp.org/www-community/vulnerabilities/Information_exposure_through_query_strings_in_url
